perpetual

/per-PECH-oo-ul/ — stress on PECH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Perpetual means continuing endlessly, or for a very long time, without stopping.

Fishermen who pass nearby describe the roar as a perpetual growl, a sound that has echoed across those waters for as long as anyone can remember.

Example

The lighthouse beam swept across the dark ocean, a perpetual light that had shone through countless storms and calm nights for over a hundred years.

Perpetual is more precise than just saying 'long-lasting' or 'enduring' because it emphasizes the idea of going on without end — a timeless, endless quality that suggests the light will continue forever, not just for a very long time.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

endless: Endless claims there is no stopping point at all, ever — an endless loop, endless space. Perpetual is slightly humbler: it means continuing without stopping for an extremely long time, perhaps forever, perhaps not. A mortgage can feel perpetual yet still end; endless allows no end even in principle.

eternal: Eternal means existing forever, outside ordinary time — a word for souls, truths, and stars. Perpetual stays inside human time: it describes earthly things that keep going without a visible end, like perpetual motion or perpetual committee meetings. Eternal belongs to philosophy; perpetual belongs to calendars that never clear.

ceaseless: Ceaseless means never pausing even once — ceaseless rain, ceaseless chatter — and it stresses the absence of any break. Perpetual stresses sheer endurance across time and can even survive interruptions: perpetual repairs stop and resume for centuries. Ceaseless noise never quiets; a perpetual quarrel can sleep for years and return.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

temporary: lasting only a limited, short time

intermittent: stopping and starting at irregular intervals

Where it sits · how close to lasting forever — brief → lengthy → constant → perpetual

brief vs. perpetual: A brief power outage is over in minutes; the hum of the city's electrical grid is perpetual, never once falling silent.

lengthy vs. perpetual: A lengthy drought may drag on for years yet still break with the next rainy season, while a perpetual desert has stayed dry beyond all memory and shows no sign of ever changing.

constant vs. perpetual: The museum guard kept a constant watch through her eight-hour shift, but the drip of water in the ancient cistern beneath the building was perpetual, sounding long before her lifetime and destined to continue long after it.

Which word fits?

Answer correctly to continue.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — per-

Prefix — per-: through, throughout, thoroughly

Root — pet-

Root — pet-: to seek, rush toward, press on (from Latin petere)

Suffix — -ual

Suffix — -ual: relating to (a form of the suffix -al)

Put it together

Put it together: Per- (through) + pet- (to rush, press on) + -ual (relating to) paints a vivid picture: something that keeps rushing on through — never pausing, never ending. Latin perpetuus meant 'continuous, unbroken,' and English kept that sense: a perpetual motion machine, perpetual complaints. Notice the root: it is the same pet- as in repetition and repetitive — one seeks again, the other presses on forever.

Use the root in a new word: impetus

Use the root in a new word: impetus: The mayor's speech gave new impetus to the recycling campaign — from Latin in- (upon) + petere (to rush at), an impetus is the push that sends something rushing forward.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Perpetual is the word to use when you want to emphasize endless duration or the sense of something continuing without end. For something that lasts a very long time but will eventually stop, 'lasting' or 'enduring' fits better. Perpetual is grander and suggests something timeless.
